Hermes is an always-on agent that learns and runs your workflows; OpenClaw is a popular personal assistant you message like a friend; Claude Code is a world-class coding agent. In the video below I show Hermes, Claude and Codex working as one system. Here’s the three-way comparison and how to combine them.

Key takeaways

- Hermes: always-on agent with memory, skills and scheduled jobs.

- OpenClaw: simple, hugely popular personal assistant via chat apps.

- Claude Code: the strongest of the three for building software.

- Best setup: use all three, each for its job.

When I need to build something — a dashboard, a tool, a site — Claude Code is the one I reach for. It’s not trying to be your always-on assistant; it’s trying to write excellent code.

## How I use all three together

- Claude Code builds the tools and automations.

- Hermes runs them on a schedule and reports back.

- OpenClaw handles quick personal tasks through chat.

- An Agent OS puts them in one dashboard with shared memory.

You can even use your Claude subscription as Hermes’s brain through a plugin — check Anthropic’s terms first.

## Which should you start with?

Start with Hermes if you want an agent that runs your business. Start with Claude Code if you mostly build software. Try OpenClaw if you want the simplest possible personal assistant. Most people end up with two or three of them.

## Costs across the three

Hermes and OpenClaw are free and open source; you pay only for the models you use, and both can run on free or local models. Claude Code needs a Claude subscription or API usage. In practice, a sensible budget is one paid Claude plan for coding and free models for Hermes’ routine work, which keeps costs low while giving you the best tool for each job.

## A workflow that uses all three

Here’s a real pattern. I ask Claude Code to build a small tool — say, a script that pulls my Search Console data and writes a summary. Hermes runs that script every Monday morning on my VPS and sends the summary to Telegram. During the week, when I need something quick — book a reminder, find a file, check a fact — I message OpenClaw or Hermes from my phone. Each agent does what it’s best at, and nothing falls through the cracks.

## Common mistakes when choosing

The most common mistake is expecting one agent to do everything. A coding agent left running as a personal assistant is overkill and expensive; a personal assistant asked to refactor a large codebase will struggle. The second mistake is ignoring safety: whichever agents you use, keep approvals on for anything that sends, buys or deletes, and don’t expose them to the public internet.

## Best choice by type of user

- Business owners: start with Hermes, add Claude Code when you need a custom tool built.

- Developers: start with Claude Code, add Hermes to run and monitor what you build.

- Personal users: OpenClaw or Hermes for everyday assistance through chat apps.

Whichever you choose, start with one real job, keep approvals on for anything risky, and expand once it’s working reliably. The best agent is the one you actually use every day, and the fastest way to find it is to test it on your own work rather than reading feature lists.

## Getting started with all three

Install Hermes first and connect Telegram, so you have an always-on agent. Add Claude Code when you need to build something. Try OpenClaw if you want a second personal assistant with a different feel. Within a week you’ll know which jobs belong to which agent, and an Agent OS can bring them together on one screen.

## The bottom line

In Hermes Agent vs OpenClaw vs Claude Code, there’s no single winner: Hermes runs, OpenClaw assists and Claude Code builds. Use each for its job.

One last thought: these tools are improving every month. Hermes added keyless setup, connectors and one-click local models in v0.22; Claude Code keeps getting stronger with each Claude release; and OpenClaw has a foundation and OpenAI’s support behind it. Rather than betting on one winner, build your workflows as skills and scripts you own, so you can move them between agents as the landscape changes.

When to use Claude Code

  • Building apps, dashboards and tools.
  • Working in large codebases.
  • Refactoring, debugging and writing tests.

When to use Hermes Agent

  • Daily briefs, inbox triage and reports on a schedule.
  • Research and content workflows delivered to your phone.
  • Tasks across many apps through connectors and plugins.
  • Running 24/7 on a VPS or Hermes Cloud.

Using them together

My favourite pattern: Claude Code builds the automation, Hermes runs it. Claude Code writes a script that pulls Search Console data and drafts a report; Hermes schedules it every Monday and sends it to Telegram. You can also give Hermes Claude as its brain through Anthropic or the subscription plugin — just check Anthropic’s terms.

See also my Hermes Agent vs Claude page for the model-versus-agent question.

Costs compared

Hermes itself is free; you can run it on free models from Nous Portal or OpenCode, or locally. Claude Code requires a Claude subscription or API usage, which is worth it if you code a lot. Many people pay for Claude for coding and run Hermes on free models for everything else.

A real example: build with Claude Code, run with Hermes

Last month I needed a weekly SEO report. I asked Claude Code to write the script: pull Search Console data, compare it with last week and highlight pages that were rising or falling. It built and tested the script in one session. Then I gave the script to Hermes, which runs it every Monday on my VPS and sends the summary to Telegram. Claude Code did the building in minutes; Hermes does the running forever.

Speed and quality

Claude Code, with Claude’s best models, produces some of the highest-quality code of any agent, especially on large or complex projects. Hermes can code too, and it’s fast on everyday scripting with the right model, but it isn’t trying to be the best pure coder. If a task is mostly about writing great code, give it to Claude Code; if it’s mostly about doing something regularly, give it to Hermes.

Who should pick which

Developers and technical founders who mainly build software should start with Claude Code. Business owners, marketers and creators who want work done automatically should start with Hermes. Anyone doing both will get the most value from using them together, ideally in one Agent OS so you can see everything in one place.

Best choice by type of user

  • Business owners: Hermes first, for daily automation; bring in Claude Code when you need something built.
  • Developers: Claude Code first, then Hermes to schedule and monitor your scripts.
  • Creators: Hermes for content workflows like turning videos into posts, Claude Code for building tools around them.
  • Agencies: both, with Hermes running client reports and Claude Code building internal tools.

Whichever you choose, start with one real job, keep approvals on for anything risky, and expand once it’s working reliably. The best agent is the one you actually use every day, and the fastest way to find it is to test it on your own work rather than reading feature lists.

Getting started

If you’re new to both, install Hermes Desktop and complete the setup chat, then give it one daily job. When you have something to build, open Claude Code in the folder for that project and describe what you want. Keep the two roles separate at first: Claude Code builds, Hermes runs. Once that feels natural, connect Claude as one of Hermes’ models for the jobs that need its quality.

The bottom line on Hermes Agent vs Claude Code

If you only remember one thing, make it this: Claude Code is where you build, and Hermes is where your work keeps running. Keep that split, route models sensibly, and you’ll get the best of both without paying for more than you need. - Quick coding jobs and prototypes.

- Testing new free models as they launch.

- Coding when your paid model is rate limited.

- Scheduled jobs and reports.

- Tasks across your apps and messaging platforms.

Install OpenCode and Hermes. In OpenCode, check which free models are available — recently DeepSeek V4.1 Flash has been a great choice. Now Hermes’ memory, skills and scheduling run on a free brain. When a free window closes, switch the profile to another free model.

Hermes is where scheduled jobs, reports and messaging workflows live. Many of my automations start as an OpenCode session and end up as a Hermes skill.

Free models can be rate limited or change without notice, so always keep a second free model ready in both tools. Review code before running it, especially if Hermes will run it on a schedule with access to your files or accounts. And keep approvals on in Hermes for anything that sends messages or deletes files.

Expecting OpenCode to run scheduled jobs on its own is one; it’s a coding agent, not an always-on assistant. Another is leaving Hermes on a paid model for every routine job when a free OpenCode model would do. items.content:
Hermes Agent vs Pi is a clash of philosophies. Pi, by Mario Zechner, is a deliberately minimal open-source agent: four core tools and a short system prompt, with everything else added through extensions. Hermes is the opposite: a full-featured agent with memory, skills, 60+ tools, scheduling and 20+ messaging platforms out of the box. In the video below I explain why Hermes changed AI agents for me. Here’s how they compare.

Key takeaways

- Pi: minimal by design — read, write, edit, bash, plus extensions.

- Hermes: batteries included — memory, skills, cron, messaging, plugins.

- Both are open source and free to run.

- Pick Pi for control and simplicity, Hermes for out-of-the-box automation.

## Two philosophies

Pi’s idea is that a small, transparent core is easier to understand, trust and extend: you start with four tools and add exactly what you need with TypeScript extensions. It’s popular with developers who want to know exactly what their agent is doing — and its components are used in other projects; Zechner has said OpenClaw uses them as its agent engine.

Hermes’ idea is that most people want an agent that works out of the box: memory that learns them, skills it writes itself, scheduled jobs, 20+ messaging platforms and a catalogue of 600 plugins. Since v0.22 you can even set it up through a chat with no API key.

A clean split: build in a coding agent (Pi, Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode), then hand the finished script to Hermes to run and monitor. That plays to each tool’s strengths.

Pi coding agent installs from npm and can sign in with subscriptions you already have, so you can be coding in minutes. Any agent that can run bash commands can also break things. Pi runs in your terminal, so review what it does. Hermes offers sandboxed terminal backends like Docker, which keep commands contained, and approvals for risky actions. Whichever you use, test on a copy of your project and keep backups.

## A practical split for coders

Here’s a split that works well: use Pi (or another dedicated coding agent) for interactive coding sessions, where you’re watching and steering. Then hand anything that needs to run regularly — scrapers, reports, monitoring scripts — to Hermes, which can schedule it, sandbox it and send you the results. You get a fast coder and a reliable operator.

- Terminal-first developers: Pi coding agent for interactive work.

- Developers who ship automations: Hermes to schedule and monitor them.

Letting any coding agent run commands on your main project without a backup is the big one. Others: expecting a minimal agent to handle scheduling and messaging without extensions, or expecting an all-round agent to match a dedicated coder on complex refactors. Pick the tool for the job, test on a copy, and keep approvals on for risky actions.

Then whichever coding agent you use — Pi, Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode — can pick up where the last one left off, and Hermes can keep running the results reliably.
